label: Closeness in Marriage
framing: Intimacy is not first a matter of the body but of being fully known and not turned away. Scripture names the goal as one flesh, two whole lives so woven together that distance in one becomes a wound in both, and it is unembarrassed that this nearness is meant to be a delight.
cultural: Our culture talks endlessly about sex and rarely about closeness, and so couples can share a bed for years and remain strangers. We have learned to perform connection and to fear the vulnerability that makes it real. The Bible is bolder than our age and tenderer, giving an entire book to the praise of married love and refusing to split the body from the soul.
historical: The Song of Solomon has been read in the synagogue and the church for over two thousand years as a celebration of married love, frank and unashamed. The Reformers in the sixteenth century recovered the goodness of the marriage bed against centuries that had treated it as a lesser thing, and the Puritans wrote without blushing of the duty and the joy of conjugal affection.
application: Closeness is rebuilt the way it was lost, in the small turnings toward each other day by day. Risk being known, telling the truth about your fear and your want, since intimacy lives only where the mask comes off. Guard the bond from the slow theft of busyness and screens. And tend the whole of it, the talking and the touching together, for in marriage the two were never meant to be pulled apart.

verses.text: For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
verses.where: The narrator steps out of the story of the first marriage to draw a lasting conclusion: a man leaves his parents, holds fast to his wife, and the two become one flesh. The site's note says this union answers the first not good in Scripture, a person alone. The chapter ends with two people naked and not ashamed, fully seen and not turned away.

verses.text: I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me; he pastures his flock among the lilies.
verses.where: When the daughters of Jerusalem offer to help her search, the woman answers that she and her beloved belong to each other. The belonging runs both ways in the same sentence. The Bible's love song has no embarrassment about desire, and no ownership in it either.

verses.text: I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone. My heart sank at his departure. I sought him, but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer.
verses.where: In this scene the woman hesitates when her beloved knocks, and by the time she opens the door he has gone. Her heart sinks, and she goes out searching. The Song is honest that love can miss its moment, and that closeness, once lost, has to be sought again.

verses.text: Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all.
verses.where: The note calls this the book's great statement: set me as a seal on your heart, for love is as strong as death, and many waters cannot quench it. A seal marked what belonged to someone and could not be broken without notice. Married love is pictured as that kind of claim, freely given and fiercely kept.

verses.text: May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth: A loving doe, a graceful fawn— may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be captivated by her love forever.
verses.where: A father warns his son that the forbidden woman's words are sweet at first and bitter in the end, and then tells him where joy is found: in the wife of his youth. The same book that warns so sternly about adultery is frank about delight in marriage. Faithfulness and pleasure are not rivals in Proverbs.

verses.text: If a man is newly married, he must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married.
verses.where: Among laws protecting the poor and the vulnerable, Moses exempts a newly married man from war and every other duty for a year. The reason given is that he may stay home and bring joy to his wife. Israel's law counted a marriage's first year as worth guarding from the demands of the nation.

verses.text: Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun—all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun.
verses.where: The Teacher has just said that the same death comes to everyone. His counsel is not despair but this: eat your bread with joy, and enjoy life with the wife you love all your fleeting days. Because life is brief, the ordinary nearness of a marriage is called a portion from God.

verses.text: In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church.
verses.where: Paul tells husbands to love their wives as their own bodies, to nourish and cherish them as Christ does the church, and he quotes Genesis 2 on the two becoming one flesh. The site's notes set out how Christians read the headship and submission in this chapter and choose no side. On every reading, the love asked of a husband is self-giving, never self-serving.

verses.text: The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value. She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.
verses.where: The book ends with a poem in praise of a wife of strength and wisdom. The first thing it says of her marriage is trust: her husband's heart trusts her, and she does him good and not harm all her days. Closeness rests on that kind of safety.

verses.text: Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.
verses.where: Hebrews closes with practical instructions: brotherly love, hospitality, remembering prisoners, honoring marriage, and freedom from the love of money. Honor for the marriage bed sits beside them as part of ordinary faithfulness. The verse guards marriage from both contempt and betrayal.

misread.taken: These verses have been used to teach that a husband, or less often a wife, has a right to sex whenever he wants it, and that a spouse who says no is disobeying God.
misread.says: The site's note on the chapter says it plainly: this must be said because these verses have been misused. Paul says each partner belongs to the other, and speaks of husband and wife in exactly the same words, which in his world set wives on equal ground. He asks for mutual consent. He gives no one permission to force, pressure or threaten, and the note calls forcing or pressuring a husband or wife into sex wrong, and abuse. The love Paul describes later in the same letter is not self-seeking.
misread.text: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control.

whole: Closeness in marriage rarely ends with a quarrel. More often it fades. Children arrive, work expands, bodies change, and two people who once could not stop talking now pass each other in the hallway with lists. For some couples the distance is mostly in the bedroom, carried in silence because neither knows how to raise it. For others it is older: a wound that never healed, shame brought in from before the marriage, or a trust that was broken. Many Christians also carry a strange double message from church, which taught them for years that sex was dangerous and then expected them to find it easy on their wedding night.

Scripture speaks about this more openly than many churches do. It begins with two people naked and unashamed, and it keeps a whole book of love poetry in the canon, with desire and delight and the pain of missed moments all set down. It calls a marriage one flesh, which means the body and the whole life together, so that distance in one place soon becomes distance everywhere. It also names what breaks closeness. Shame makes people hide, as the first couple hid. Selfishness turns the gift into a demand. Unfaithfulness, even in the heart, divides what God joined. And our own busyness quietly teaches a marriage that everything else comes first.

The wisdom here is mutual and patient. Paul's word to married Christians is that each belongs to the other, in the same words for both, and that nothing is to be taken that is not freely given. Proverbs and Ecclesiastes tell husbands and wives to delight in each other on purpose, as part of the portion God gives in a brief life, and Israel's law guarded a new marriage's first year so that joy could take root. Closeness grows where it is safe to be known: where the hard conversation can happen without contempt, where the body is cared for rather than used, and where a couple will seek help together, from a pastor or a counselor or a doctor, rather than let silence decide. If you are being pressured or forced, that is not a problem of intimacy; it is wrong, it is not your fault, and safety comes first.

Underneath all of it is a larger picture. Paul says that the one-flesh union speaks of Christ and the church, a love that gives itself first and is not ashamed of the people it loves. A marriage will not reach that perfectly, and no couple should measure themselves against a fantasy. But a husband and wife who keep turning toward each other, slowly and with forgiveness, are living inside a story bigger than their own, one in which being fully known and fully loved is not a fragile hope but the shape of the world to come.

differ.share: Christians agree that sex is God's good gift, that it belongs within the faithfulness of marriage, that husbands and wives give themselves to each other freely and equally, and that coercion within marriage is always wrong.

views.name: Open to life in each act
views.body: Catholic teaching holds that each marital act should remain open to the gift of life and rejects artificial contraception, while permitting couples to space children by natural family planning. Holders of this view see the unity of love and life in marriage as part of the gift itself.

views.name: Contraception within marriage
views.body: Most Protestant churches and many Orthodox Christians permit contraception within marriage, holding that a couple may in good conscience plan the number and spacing of their children while welcoming children as a blessing.

differ.after: The site's note on Genesis 38 records both readings of Onan's sin there: some traditions have read it as teaching against contraception as such, and others take the sin to be his refusal of his duty to his brother's widow. All of these churches call husbands and wives to generosity, faithfulness and mutual care, and all of them welcome children as a gift from God.

deep.sit: What is one small, unhurried thing you could do this week that would tell your husband or wife you want to be close, not because it is owed, but because you choose them?

prayer.lead: Two lines from Psalm 90 that a husband and wife can pray together, especially after a hard season.
prayer.text: Satisfy us in the morning with Your loving devotion, that we may sing for joy and be glad all our days. Make us glad for as many days as You have afflicted us, for as many years as we have seen evil.

careLines.text: Forcing or pressuring a husband or wife into sex is wrong, and it is abuse.
If you are being pressured or forced in your marriage, it is not your fault, and these verses do not ask you to submit to it.
If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first.
Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
